pages.angle: what a service engagement actually covers, and where it stops
pages.direct_answer: Webinar production services cover the technical and editorial work of running a live webinar: broadcast setup, rehearsal, live show-calling, speaker support, and recording delivery. West Peek produces moderated webinars in the $2,500 to $7,500 range, scaled by speaker count, rehearsal depth, and whether the session is single-run or part of a series.
sections: What is included in a production engagement

A production engagement is scoped around the run of show, not the software. It covers pre-production (format design, speaker briefing, dry run), live execution (broadcast control, lower thirds, speaker cueing, Q&A moderation support, failover monitoring), and post-production (recording cleanup, chaptering, asset handoff). The platform licence is usually yours; the operating capability is what you are buying.
Where the scope usually stops

Most engagements exclude audience acquisition, list building, and post-event nurture. They also exclude content authorship - a producer will shape a run of show and coach delivery, but will not write your subject-matter argument. Clarify slide production ownership early; it is the single most common scope dispute.
What a $2,500 webinar differs from a $7,500 one

Price moves with speaker count, rehearsal depth, and failover posture. A single-speaker session with one rehearsal and a straightforward deck sits at the low end. Multi-speaker panels, live demos, interpretation, or a redundant backup stream sit at the high end. Large executive summits and conferences are a different category and run $10,000 to $50,000 and above.
What goes wrong

The failures are rarely creative. They are an unrehearsed speaker joining from an untested network, a demo environment that was never load-checked, a moderator with no cue discipline, and no rehearsed failover path when a presenter drops. Ask any prospective producer what happens in the first thirty seconds after a speaker's connection dies - the answer separates operators from vendors.
How to decide whether you need this

If the webinar is internal, low-stakes, and single-speaker, your team can likely run it. Bring in production when the audience is external and the cost of a visible failure is high: analyst briefings, customer launches, executive appearances, regulated content, or anything being recorded for reuse.
faqs: What do webinar production services cost?

Do I need my own webinar platform?
Usually yes. The platform licence typically stays with you; production supplies the broadcast control, rehearsal, live operation, and continuity layer on top of it.
How far ahead should a webinar be booked?

Two to three weeks is workable for a straightforward single-speaker session. Multi-speaker panels and anything with a live demo need longer, because rehearsal availability rather than production capacity is the constraint.

pages.angle: how to evaluate and choose a production partner
pages.direct_answer: A virtual event production company runs the broadcast, rehearsal, and live operation of online events so the host can focus on content. Evaluate one on rehearsal discipline, failover plan, and show-calling experience rather than platform logos. West Peek has produced over 400 events since 2020 for Fortune 500 companies and top business schools.
sections: What a production company actually supplies

Three things: a rehearsed run of show, an operator calling the live show, and a continuity plan for when something fails. Everything else - platform, branding, registration - is either yours or commodity. Companies that lead with software features are selling you a tool you could licence yourself.
Questions that separate operators from resellers

Ask who is on the call during the live show and what each person does. Ask what the failover path is when the primary stream degrades. Ask how many rehearsals are included and what happens if a speaker misses theirs. Ask for the run-of-show document from a comparable event with the client details removed. Vague answers to any of these are disqualifying.
Stack, and why it matters less than you think

West Peek runs role-based infrastructure: StreamYard for broadcast control, LiveKit for real-time venue infrastructure, and Daily for backup continuity. The specific tools matter far less than whether the team has a rehearsed answer for each failure mode. A strong operator on ordinary tooling beats a weak one on premium tooling every time.
Pricing you should expect

Moderated webinars run $2,500 to $7,500. Executive summits, multi-track conferences, and hybrid productions run $10,000 to $50,000 and above. Anyone quoting a flat rate without asking about speaker count, rehearsal expectations, or failover requirements has not scoped your event.
Where in-house is the better answer

If you run frequent, format-identical, internal sessions, build the capability in-house - the economics favour it past roughly two events a month. Bring in a production company for irregular, high-stakes, externally visible events where the failure cost is asymmetric.
